aliases.name: Caointeach
aliases.meaning: regional variant; appears outside the homes of the soon-to-die wearing a green shawl

description.summary: A female death-portent spirit of the Scottish Highlands, associated particularly with certain clans, who weeps at waterfalls, streams, and lonely places before a death — most famously before the Massacre of Glencoe.
description.full: The Caoineag (Scottish Gaelic for 'the weeper') is a female spirit of the Scottish Highlands whose lamentation is heard before deaths, especially violent or mass deaths. She is normally invisible and is heard wailing at waterfalls, in glens, by streams, and on mountainsides. Unlike the related bean nighe (the 'washer at the ford'), the Caoineag cannot be approached, questioned, or compelled to grant wishes. She is closely associated with specific clans, including Clan MacDonald of Glencoe, whose Caoineag was said to wail repeatedly the night before the 1692 Massacre of Glencoe. The closely related Caointeach is recorded in Islay tradition as a green-shawled figure heard outside the homes of those about to die. The figure is documented in Alexander Carmichael's Carmina Gadelica and in Edward Dwelly's Scottish Gaelic dictionary, and is part of a broader Gaelic family of female death-portent beings that includes the Irish bean sídhe (banshee).

etymology.origin: Scottish Gaelic caoin- ('to weep, lament') with the feminine agent suffix -eag.
etymology.first_use: Recorded in Scottish Gaelic oral tradition; published English-language records in the 19th and early 20th centuries (Carmichael, Campbell, Dwelly).

related_phenomena.name: Bean sídhe (Banshee)
related_phenomena.description: Irish female death-portent spirit; the closest cognate to the Caoineag

related_phenomena.name: Bean nighe
related_phenomena.description: Scottish Gaelic 'washer at the ford' — a related, but distinct, death-portent figure who can be approached

related_phenomena.name: Caointeach
related_phenomena.description: Islay variant of the Caoineag, appearing in a green shawl

features.description: The Caoineag is generally heard but not seen
Distinctive sustained lamentation in the manner of a Gaelic funeral keen
The Islay Caointeach is described in tradition as wearing a green shawl

physical.morphology: Typically incorporeal in tradition; the rare physical descriptions belong to the Caointeach variant.

abilities.description: Hears or 'knows' an approaching death and laments before it occurs, particularly mass or violent deaths affecting her associated clan
Her keen carries through glens and across waterways

habitat_preference: lonely places near a clan's territory
patterns: Heard before deaths, especially violent or mass deaths
Associated with specific Highland clans rather than individual households
Cannot be approached or questioned, unlike the bean nighe

range.description: Scottish Highlands and the Hebrides, with strong attestation in Lochaber (Glencoe), Argyll, and Islay.

hotspots.name: Glen Coe
hotspots.notes: Site associated with the Caoineag of Clan MacDonald of Glencoe in oral tradition.

first_recorded.source: Alexander Carmichael, Carmina Gadelica (1900); the underlying oral tradition is older.

peak_activity_periods.description: Caoineag traditions current among Gaelic-speaking Highland communities
Period of folklore collection (Carmichael, Dwelly, Campbell of Islay)

origins.cultural_roots: Scottish Gaelic Highland and Hebridean tradition; part of the broader Gaelic complex of female death-portent figures shared with Ireland.
origins.earliest_accounts: Oral tradition recorded in 19th- and early-20th-century folklore collections; the Glencoe association dates the tradition at least to the late 17th century.
origins.folklore_connections: Cognate with the Irish bean sídhe (banshee); related to but distinct from the Scottish bean nighe and the Manx caointeagh.

timeline.event: Massacre of Glencoe; later Highland tradition holds that the Caoineag of Clan MacDonald wailed nightly before the killings
timeline.significance: The most-cited single legend involving the Caoineag
timeline.source: Highland oral tradition; recorded in Carmichael (1900) and later sources

timeline.event: Alexander Carmichael publishes Carmina Gadelica, including material on the Caoineag
timeline.significance: First major scholarly publication of the tradition in English
timeline.source: Carmichael, A., Carmina Gadelica vol. II

timeline.event: Edward Dwelly's Illustrated Gaelic-English Dictionary appears, defining caoineag among Scottish Gaelic supernatural terms
timeline.significance: Lexical attestation in the standard Gaelic dictionary

history.modern_era: The Caoineag survives as a name in Scottish folklore reference works, walking-tour interpretation in Glencoe, and contemporary Gaelic-revival literature. Few or no modern first-person 'sightings' are claimed; the figure today functions chiefly as a culturally embedded death-omen tradition rather than a live cryptozoological or paranormal claim.

documentary.name: Carmina Gadelica entry
documentary.description: Alexander Carmichael's late-19th-century field collection of Hebridean and Highland Gaelic tradition includes references to the Caoineag.
documentary.analysis: Standard primary source for late-19th-century Highland folklore; Carmichael's editorial method has been critically reassessed by later scholars but remains foundational.

paranormal.name: Tutelary clan-spirit
paranormal.description: The Caoineag is interpreted in tradition as a guardian or kin-spirit attached to a specific clan, whose lamentation gives warning of approaching disaster.
evidence_cited: Other clan-attached caoineag stories recorded in 19th-c. folklore

skeptical.name: Folkloric explanation of natural sounds
skeptical.description: The Caoineag's keen is sometimes explained as the wind in glens, distant animal cries, or the sound of fast-moving water — natural sounds heard at night and culturally interpreted as a death portent.
evidence_cited: Comparative studies of acoustic interpretations in death-portent traditions

stories: The Caoineag of Glencoe wails before the 1692 massacre
The Islay Caointeach in the green shawl
folklore.beliefs: In Highland Gaelic tradition, the Caoineag is understood as a real spirit-being whose lamentation warns of impending death. She is feared and respected rather than venerated.

indigenous.significance: The Caoineag is part of a living Gaelic supernatural inheritance closely linked to clan identity and to the cultural practice of keening (caoineadh) at funerals.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Highland clan traditions surrounding the Caoineag are connected to specific historical traumas (notably the Glencoe Massacre); the figure should be discussed with respect for descendant communities.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Use Gaelic spellings and acknowledge primary Gaelic sources where possible; avoid conflating the Caoineag with the Irish banshee, which is a distinct cognate tradition.

other: Mentioned in Highland walking-tour interpretation around Glencoe

researchers.name: Alexander Carmichael
researchers.contribution: Compiled the foundational late-19th-century record of Highland and Hebridean tradition (Carmina Gadelica)

researchers.name: Edward Dwelly
researchers.contribution: Standard Gaelic dictionary including supernatural terms

organizations.name: School of Scottish Studies, University of Edinburgh
organizations.focus: Scholarly study of Scottish Gaelic oral tradition, including supernatural beings

research.ongoing_studies: Academic study of the Caoineag is ongoing within Celtic Studies and Scottish folkloristics, generally as part of broader work on death-portent figures in Gaelic tradition.
